rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 and 3 - one-season (2013) in-situ monitoring of soil water content, groundwater level, maize growth and weather in three flood-irrigated maize fields, with HYDRUS-1D calibrated/validated on measured SWC (Fig. 4, RMSE 0.010-0.054). Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 2 - scenario simulations with the field-validated model show optimized schedules reduce irrigation by 65/45/13% (OI-1) and 84/61/23% (OI-2) in NFW/OF/NFD while relative transpiration is maintained or raised; Section 4.4 reports Ta/(P+I) rising from 0.79, 0.48, 0.64 to up to 2.56, 1.05, 0.86. Q4: Table 2, Fig. 5 and Section 4.3-4.4 - the model quantifies deep percolation, actual evaporation, capillary rise and Ta/Tp, showing water saving arises through cutting deep percolation (by 428, 329, 162 mm under OI-2) and nonproductive Ea. Q5: Table 1-2, Fig. 9 - the effect is evaluated and reported separately for three fields with distinct soil profiles/groundwater settings (loamy OF with deep GWL, sandy NFD with deep GWL, sandy-over-loam NFW with shallow GWL), with field-specific optimized schedules. Q7: Abstract, Section 4.4 and Conclusions - authors state from their results that soil texture and GWL must be considered in schedule design (frequent small irrigations required on sandy NFD, fewer larger ones on loamy OF; reliance on capillary rise in NFW requires attention to secondary salinization from slightly saline groundwater). Q8: Section 4.4 - limitations stated: no feedback of root water uptake on crop growth (same growth indexes used for all scenarios), no feedback of rescheduled irrigation on GWL, which probably overestimates groundwater contribution and water-saving potential; also one-season data and simplified 1-D treatment of plastic mulch (Section 4.1).
rows.notes: The water-saving effect of the optimized schedules comes from scenario simulations that were never implemented in the field; the model itself was calibrated and validated against measured SWC in the same fields under the current schedule, which is why Q2 is rated yes, but the optimized-schedule outcomes themselves were not checked against observations. Triangulation absent: the effect rests on one modelling method. Representativeness is borderline (three fields in one region, one crop, one season; NFW and NFD both sandy at depth) but the authors treat them as three distinct soil/GWL settings and report each separately. Only RMSE/MAE validation errors reported; no dispersion or uncertainty propagation for the water-saving figures. The study uses a physically based model (HYDRUS-1D) for schedule optimization, not an app; the passage itself does not mention an app, so technology_mismatch is not flagged, but the review's 'app_scheduling' label is a loose fit.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-season (2013) study of three flood-irrigated maize fields in the Heihe River basin, NW China, combining field monitoring with HYDRUS-1D simulation to quantify water balance and propose optimized irrigation schedules.
